messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Ship Captain
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 42, Daniel had spent most of his adult life on the water and had built a reputation as a steady ship captain, the kind of man his crew trusted when weather turned or machinery failed. The event that broke that certainty happened eighteen months ago in a foreign port during a politically tense cargo transfer. A blast went off on the dock near the loading area, close enough that he felt the shock through the deck before he fully registered the sound. Men in uniforms flooded the scene afterward—some military, some local police—and in the confusion he watched cargo containers swing, equipment topple, and loose objects get hurled by the force of the explosion and the panicked movement that followed. He remembered the violent crack of it, the sight of things flying across the dock, and the uniforms converging while nobody seemed in control. What stayed with him almost as strongly as the blast itself was the aftermath: no clear answers, no sense that anyone responsible had been held to account, only official statements and denials that left him convinced the people behind it had faced no consequences.

In the weeks afterward, Daniel tried to keep working as if discipline would carry him through, but he had come to believe that thinking directly about that day would overwhelm him. He pushed the memory away whenever it began to surface, telling himself that if he let it in fully he would not be able to handle it. At the same time, the way the authorities had managed the aftermath hardened something in him. He became certain other people could not be relied on to keep anyone safe, not officials, not security personnel, not even people who claimed to know what they were doing. Those beliefs changed how he moved through the world. He began avoiding unfamiliar places whenever possible because he felt he could not judge the danger there for himself, and when he had to enter a restaurant, waiting area, or ferry terminal, he immediately scanned for the safest seat—something with a wall behind him, a clear view of the exits, distance from strangers. Nights became especially difficult because he felt he needed to stay alert; falling asleep seemed like letting his guard down in a world where nobody else could be counted on.

Those same beliefs also made the reminders of the disaster feel charged long before he consciously named them. A sudden bang on the street or a dropped metal object on the ship could jolt him into the same bodily alarm as the blast on the dock. Seeing police or military uniforms no longer read as reassuring; because he no longer believed authority meant protection, the sight of them brought back the chaos and helpless anger of that day. Even something as ordinary as a person throwing a tool or tossing a line hard across the deck could freeze him for a second, his mind snagging on the image of objects flying after the explosion.

As months passed, Daniel’s constant sense of danger began shaping what he did to get through each day. On board, he watched people closely for signs that someone might be volatile or unsafe, tracking faces and movements more than he used to. In ports he did not know, he sometimes stayed back from tasks he would once have handled himself, giving up responsibilities he considered important because it felt safer to let others deal with loading areas, security checkpoints, or meetings ashore. He told himself this was prudence. His wife saw it differently when he came home and described stepping away from parts of the job he had once taken pride in. To blunt the tension and restless alertness, he also started gambling more often—online in his cabin, sometimes in port—chasing the narrow tunnel of concentration and excitement that briefly drowned out the vigilance.

None of this brought him relief for long. Each time he handed off a duty or retreated from a place he could not fully assess, it seemed to confirm his view that the world was unsafe and that he was right not to depend on anyone else. The gambling left him ashamed and more distrustful of himself, while the fact that it had become one of the few ways he could shut his mind off only deepened his fear that if he ever stopped controlling his thoughts, the whole memory would break over him. Living in this guarded way also kept proving to him that danger was everywhere: every room needed to be evaluated, every stranger watched, every night defended against sleep. The tighter he held himself, the more convinced he became that he was surrounded by risks and abandoned by systems that were supposed to provide accountability.

By the time he came for help, Daniel’s marriage was strained by his withdrawal and by arguments about money he had lost gambling. At work, delegating out of fear rather than judgment had started to affect how he saw himself as a captain. What finally pushed him into treatment was a recent incident in port when a crane operator dropped cargo with a thunderous bang and a security officer ran toward the commotion in uniform; Daniel froze, then abruptly left the area and turned command over to his first mate. He said he could no longer pretend this was just stress. What frightened him most was the idea that he was becoming a man who could not trust anyone, could not sleep, could not do his job, and could not let himself think about why. What he hoped, cautiously, was not to erase what happened but to stop living as if the explosion were still about to occur.
